column4: The section’s root ق د ر moves between power and measure; Jonah’s “ظن أن لن نقدر عليه” repeats the claim’s exact construction, then his call in darkness shows where that presumption turns.

The section’s 90:7 question imagines no one saw the man; here people had thought their hearing, eyes, and skins would not testify, but the verse says they wrongly thought Allah did not know their deeds.
The section treats eyes as measured parts and asks whether anyone saw the man; this verse names hearing, sight, and skin as witnesses to deeds, giving those created parts an answering role.
The section’s dictionary image measures hide before cutting it, while this verse has skins speak and says Allah created people the first time; it joins formed body, skin, and speech in one scene.
The section’s 90:7 asks whether the man thinks nobody saw him; “ألم يعلم بأن الله يرى” directly reverses that assumption and identifies the unseen observer.
The section’s “أحد” is nobody in the man’s boast that no one can overpower him; here “لا يعذب عذابه أحد” turns that negation around, saying no one can punish as the Lord does.
The section’s negative “أحد” means nobody can reach the man; here “ولا يوثق وثاقه أحد” says nobody binds as the Lord binds, setting an opposite limit on power.
The section explains “أحد” in 90:5 as “anyone” under negation; “الله أحد” gives the same named word its divine singular sense, answering the boast’s imagined absence of an overpowering one.
The section sets 90:3’s parent and offspring against the declaration “لم يلد ولم يولد”; the created line of birth has a boundary in the One who neither begets nor is born.

The section explicitly gives the ق د ر branch “ومن قدر عليه رزقه” as provision narrowed; this verse uses it and quotes the person’s conclusion, “ربي أهانن,” showing how he misreads an allotted measure.

The section points to 89:16 as one response to measured provision; this preceding ayah supplies the paired ease, which the person reads as honor (“ربي أكرمن”), exposing both judgments as human interpretations.
The section’s dictionary note labels human تقدير as thinking through what to do; this person “فكر وقدر,” making his deliberate calculation a concrete instance of that sense.
The section connects the person’s own estimate to the root ق د ر; “فقتل كيف قدر” condemns this human measuring, marking its limit beside the Creator’s measure.
The section’s “أَيَحْسَبُ” challenges a person’s unsupported estimate; this repeats the question and names his imagined limit—whether God can gather his bones.
The section calls the eyes, tongue, and lips measured parts; this answer to 75:3 says God can even proportion the fingertips (“نسوي بنانه”), making bodily formation the proof of power.
The section asks whether a person thinks no one can measure or constrain him; this asks whether he thinks he will be left “سدى,” connecting that presumption to having no governing purpose or limit.
The section’s root خ ل ق is framed as straight measure; “خلق فسوى” pairs creation with fashioning into due form, making the measured-form image explicit.
The section follows 90:4 creation with 90:5 power and 90:10 guidance; “قدر فهدى” directly joins measured determination to guidance in that sequence.
Moses describes the Lord as the one who gave each thing its created form (“أعطى كل شيء خلقه”) and then guided it; this joins the section’s shaped creation to its later guidance.
The section’s root ق د ر includes assigning a measure; “من نطفة خلقه فقدره” says the human was created from a drop and then measured, a close parallel to the measured human form.
The section calls the eyes, tongue, and lips measured parts; this verse says the created human was made hearing and seeing, tying bodily faculties to human creation.
After 76:2’s created, hearing and seeing human, this verse says “إنا هديناه السبيل”; it completes a creation-to-guidance sequence like the one the section sees in 90:4–10.
The section’s root خ ل ق means measured making and its ق د ر root names measure; “خلق كل شيء فقدره تقديرا” states both actions together.
The section treats creation as proportioned measure; “إنا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر” states that all created things are made according to measure.
The section’s dictionary sense of ق د ر is a thing’s reached extent and limit; “وكل شيء عنده بمقدار” places every matter within a measure held by God.
The section connects ق د ر to measured provision and each person’s allotment; this says what is sent down comes “بقدر معلوم,” making provision’s measure explicit.
The section’s root ق د ر names measured bounds; “قد جعل الله لكل شيء قدرا” states that God has set a measure for everything.
The section imagines a hide measured before it is cut and says the human’s eyes and other parts were measured; this says God created, proportioned, and balanced the person (“فسواك فعدلك”).
The section says “ألم نجعل” belongs to the same work as creation and names eyes as made parts; this verse uses جعل for hearing, sight, and hearts after fashioning the human.
The section’s ق س م dictionary note defines dividing into shares; “نحن قسمنا بينهم معيشتهم” applies that division to people’s livelihoods, joining allotment to provision.
The section labels the ق د ر branch “ومن قدر عليه رزقه” as narrowed provision; this repeats that wording and commands spending from what was given within that limit.
The section links measure to each person’s provision; this says provision is sent down “بقدر ما يشاء,” making its measured distribution a divine act.
The section’s secondary dictionary form الخلاق means a share; this verse says the buyer has no “خلاق” in the Hereafter, using that same share sense.
The section labels الخلاق as an allotted share; “لا خلاق لهم في الآخرة” uses the same word for those with no share in the Hereafter.
The section’s dictionary gloss for الخلاق is a person’s نصيب, or share; this verse explicitly assigns “نصيب” to men and women, making an individual portion concrete.
The section says each person’s share is measured; this verse assigns specified fractions to heirs and calls them an obligation from God, a legal example of apportioned shares.
The section’s share image is an allotment measured for each person; this verse gives spouses and siblings fixed fractions, showing that portions can be precisely set.
The section’s share image is a measured portion for each person; this final inheritance ruling specifies fractions for siblings and completes another instance of divided shares.
The section’s dictionary image measures leather before cutting it into a waterskin; this verse describes cattle hides made into portable dwellings, showing hide shaped for a practical use.
The section’s root ق د ر joins measure and limit; the sun’s course is called “تقدير العزيز العليم,” a particular created order governed by measure.
The section names ق د ر as measure and boundary; “على الموسع قدره وعلى المقتر قدره” sets a financial obligation according to each person’s means, a specific application of measured capacity.
The section’s ق د ر branch includes constricted provision; this contrasts God’s expansion of provision with “ويقدر,” showing that the root’s measure sense also governs livelihood.
The section identifies the ق د ر root’s provision sense as narrowing what is given; this says God expands provision for some and “يقدر” for others.
The section connects ق د ر with measured provision; after Qarun’s wealth is swallowed, observers say Allah “يبسط الرزق ... ويقدر,” reading wealth as allotted rather than self-secured.
The section says every person’s share is measured and links ق د ر to provision; this states that God expands livelihood or “يقدر له” for His servants.
The section’s ق د ر root includes power and measure; this asks whether people see that God expands provision and “يقدر,” grounding human limits in divine allocation.
The section links measured power and provision through ق د ر; this says God expands livelihood and “يقدر,” while most people do not know the source of that measure.
The section’s root ق د ر includes narrowing provision; this says God expands it or “يقدر له,” then promises replacement for what people spend.
The section joins qadr with assigned provision; this asks whether people know that God expands provision and “يقدر,” a repeated statement of divinely measured livelihood.
The section describes ق د ر as measure and limit; this verse says God expands provision or “يقدر” and closes by calling Him knowing of all things.
The section’s ق س م root includes dividing and assigning portions; “فالمقسمات أمرا” names those who apportion affairs, extending that image to the distribution of commands.
The section’s 90:7 challenges the thought that no one saw the man; these people hide from other people but “ولا يستخفون من الله,” distinguishing human secrecy from divine sight.
The section names eyes as created parts and asks whether anyone saw the person; this says God knows furtive glances and what hearts conceal, joining sight to hidden acts.
The section’s man assumes he is beyond another’s power or sight; this says the Creator knows what the self whispers, extending the limit from visible acts to private thought.
The section’s root خ ل ق describes measured making; this neighboring description says God perfected what He created and began human creation from clay, preparing the formed human of 32:8–9.
The section includes the parent and child in its whole-surah context and treats the human as created form; this verse places human offspring in a sequence beginning from an extract of fluid.
The section describes the eyes as parts made for a human; this says people emerge from their mothers’ wombs knowing nothing and are given hearing, sight, and hearts.
The section’s “خلقنا الإنسان” image is measured human creation; this verse likewise says the Merciful created the human, introducing the speech faculty in 55:4.
The section names a tongue and lips among the human’s measured parts, and its man speaks his claim; “علمه البيان” connects those organs to articulate expression.
The section sees bodily features as measured parts of a created human; this says God created the human “في أحسن تقويم,” adding the image of a form made in due proportion.

The section distinguishes the ح س ب root’s counting sense from a person’s mistaken supposition; these people “يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا” while their worldly effort is lost, a concrete false self-assessment.
The section labels ح س ب as counting or estimating; here the sun and moon are made “حسبانا,” so celestial order itself supplies a reckoning against human guesswork.
The section connects ق د ر with measured limits and ح س ب with counting; the moon is set in phases so people know years and reckoning, linking measured creation to human counting.
The section names ح س ب as counting; this says the alternation of night and day lets people know the number of years and reckoning, an ordered count rather than mere supposition.
The section contrasts human supposition with measured order and names the root ح س ب; “الشمس والقمر بحسبان” makes the sun and moon move by a reckoning.
The section’s ق د ر root names power as well as measure; this asks whether the Creator of the heavens and earth is able to recreate people, turning the claim of limited power against itself.
The section labels خ ل ق’s source sense as straight measure and ق س م as dividing shares; this calls the self-serving assignment “قسمة ضيزى,” a crooked division, reversing that straight measure.
The section’s ق س م root denotes division into shares; this verse names “القسمة” of an estate and directs that nearby relatives, orphans, and the poor receive provision from it.
After the fixed portions in 4:11–12, this verse calls them “حدود الله”; it makes the section’s measure-as-limit concrete in the laws of allotted shares.
The section describes the eyes, tongue, and lips as measured parts of a created human; this says God forms people in the wombs as He wills, a specific image of bodily shaping.
The section distinguishes the ح س ب root’s counting from supposition and describes a person who presumes no one can constrain him; this asks whether people think they will be left untested.
Following 29:2’s question about expecting no trial, this verse says earlier peoples were tested; it supplies the actual limit that the preceding presumption denies.
The section’s ح س ب root includes supposing and its خ ل ق image is purposeful measured creation; this asks whether people thought they were created in vain and would not return to God.
The section’s man presumes no one can set a limit on him; this places just scales on the Day of Resurrection and says no soul is wronged, even by a mustard-seed weight.
The section’s 90:7 challenges the thought that no one sees the person; this says a person will see even an atom’s weight of good, giving smallest deeds a visible consequence.
Where the section’s man presumes his acts escape notice, this says he will see even an atom’s weight of evil, completing the paired accounting of deeds.
The section’s image of measure and assigned limits extends to judgment here: “والوزن يومئذ الحق” makes weighing the standard on that Day.
Following 7:8’s true weighing, this verse says those whose scales are heavy succeed and those whose scales are light lose themselves; it gives the outcome of measured deeds.
The section’s share image is an allotted portion of provision; this orders people to give its due on harvest, making a claim on measured produce explicit.
The section says shares are assigned by measure; this divides captured goods by specifying a fifth for God, the Messenger, and named recipients.
